say: Do not set a volume threshold independently of incremental savings over a route sheet. The supplied transport notice supports testing changing information, not hotel demand. My proposed screening gate—not an observed benchmark—is 30 relevant questions per hotel per week and 60 seconds saved per question versus a simple route sheet, with zero verified route/date errors. That implies 30 minutes saved weekly. uncertainty: Some Centrs-based SSE students repeatedly miss suitable concerts or spend unwanted time checking listings; ask prospective participants about their most recent discovery attempt and existing alternatives.

A free, checked shortlist offers enough incremental value to prompt voluntary repeat reading. Propose inviting ten students, spending under €20, and passing only if four explicitly confirm reading or request a second shortlist without individual reminders; do not rely on passive open tracking.

Students might eventually pay for saved effort, or organisers might pay for labelled promotion, but neither payer hypothesis has direct support in the supplied receipts. Test these separately after repeat usefulness, without treating free engagement as willingness to pay.
Frequency and severity of the target students' discovery problem, preferred genres and current discovery channels; no customer contact or testing has occurred.
A workable definition of nearby and enough fresh qualifying concerts to sustain daily delivery.
dissent: Existing listings or friends may solve discovery adequately; a curated shortlist could add little.
One dated concert listing cannot justify a daily habit. A weekly shortlist may fit supply better; withhold unverified picks rather than filling gaps with unrelated events.
Organiser-funded promotion could conflict with reader trust and impartial selection; it should not be assumed to finance the service.
